<!-- head-1: body_md -->
\cite{Prolubnikov1}\textbf{.} \textit{The relation $x_j^{k-1}\!=\! 0$, $x_j^k\!\neq\! 0$ holds if and only if the vertex $j\!\in\! V$ is first reached in the traversal of the graph $G$ from the vertex $s$ at exactly the $k$-th iteration, corresponding to the $k$-th iteration of the numerical method under consideration.}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Unlike the stationary methods considered in \cite{Prolubnikov1} (Theorem~1), theoretically, it is possible that $d_j^k\!=\!0$ even when $k\!\ge\!\ell(i,j)$. This can occur in exact arithmetic because contributions from vertex~$i$ to vertex~$j$ along different walks may have alternating signs and sum to zero. Although the number of such walks grows exponentially at each iteration, to have $d_j^k\!=\!0$ when $k\!\ge\!\ell(i,j)$, this growth must be counterbalanced by the exponential decay of the weights of long walks (e.g., due to matrix normalization), which prevents unbounded error amplification.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
{\it If $\mathrm{supp}(b)\!=\!\{i\}$ and $\ell(i,j)\!>\!k$, then $d_j^k\!=\!0$ and $\varepsilon_j^k\!=\!0$.}
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
We proceed by induction. Base case. For $k\!=\!1$, the basic CG recurrence relations ($d^1 = r^1 + \beta_1 d^0$, $r^1 = b - \alpha_0 Ab$, $d^0 = b$) yield
$$d_j^1=(1+\beta_1)b_j-\alpha_0(Ab)_j.$$
If $\ell(i,j)\!>\!1$, then $a_{ji}\!=\!0$ and $b_j\!=\!0$, hence
$$d_j^1\!=-\alpha_0\!(Ab)_j\!=-\alpha_0\!\sum\limits_{(j,t)\in E}^n a_{jt}b_t=-\alpha_0\cdot a_{ji}\cdot b_i=0.$$
For $k\!=\!2$:
$$d_j^2=(1+\beta_2)d_j^1-\beta_1d_j^0-\alpha_1(Ad^1)_j.$$
If $\ell(i,j)\!>\!2$, then $d_j^1\!=\!0$ (by the base case) and $d_j^0\!=\!b_j\!=\!0$. Since
$$(Ad^1)_j=\sum\limits_{(j,t)\in E}a_{jt}d_t^1\eqno(10)$$
and in the sum on the right, nonzero terms can correspond only to those $t$ for which $d_t^1\!\neq\!0$. However, if $\ell(i,j)\!>\!2$, for any such $t$ the corresponding factors~$a_{jt}$ in~(10) are equal to zero, since otherwise there would exist a path~$w\!=\!\{(i,t),(t,j)\}$ of length~$2$ in the matrix graph, which does not exist for $k\!=\!2$, according to the condition of the lemma. Consequently, $d_j^2\!=\!0$.

Inductive hypothesis: suppose the statement of Lemma~1 holds for all values less than $k$. We show that it also holds when $\ell(i,j)\!>\!k$. By the inductive hypothesis, in~(9) we have: $d_j^{k-1}\!=\!0$, $d_j^{k-2}\!=\!0$, and
$$(Ad^{k-1})_j=\sum\limits_{(j,t)\in E}a_{jt}d_t^{k-1},$$
where in the sum on the right, nonzero terms are possible only for those $t$ such that $d_t^{k-1}\!\neq\!0$. For such $t$, by the contrapositive of the inductive hypothesis, $\ell(i,t)\!\le\!k\!-\!1$. If for such $t$ we had $a_{jt}\!\neq\!0$, this would imply the existence of a path from $i$ to $j$ of length $k$. But by the condition $\ell(i,j)\!>\!k$. Consequently, no such $a_{jt}$ exist, and $d_j^k\!=\!0$.

Finally, since all components $d_j^{k-1}$, $d_j^{k-2}$, and $(Ad^{k-1})_j$ entering the recurrence for $d_j^k$ are exactly zero, the corresponding floating-point operations also yield machine zero, and no round-off error is generated or propagated into this component. Hence, $\varepsilon_j^k\!=\!0$. \qed
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- head-5: body_md -->
$d^k=\sum\limits_{i=1}^nd^k|_i$, $\varepsilon^k=\sum\limits_{i=1}^n\varepsilon^k|_i$.
<!-- end head-5 -->
<!-- head-6: body_md -->
To simplify the notation, consider the case where $\mathrm{supp}(b)\!=\!\{1,2\}$:
$$b\!=\!(b_1,b_2,0,\dots,0)\!=\! b|_1+b|_2,$$
where $b|_1\!=\!b_1\cdot e_1$, $b|_2\!=\!b_2\cdot e_2$. We prove the statement of the lemma for such $b$ by induction.

Base case. Since $d^0|_1\!=\! b|_1$ and $d^0|_2\!=\! b|_2$, for $k\!=\!1$, expression~(4) takes the form:
$$d^1=(d^0|_1+d^0|_2)-\alpha_0A(d^0|_1+d^0|_2)=(d^0|_1-\alpha_0Ad^0|_1)+(d^0|_2-\alpha_0Ad^0|_2)=$$ $$=d^1|_1+d^1|_2.$$
For $k\!=\!2$:
$$d^2=(1+\beta_2)d^1-\beta_1d^0-\alpha_1Ad^1=$$ $$=(1+\beta_2)(d^1|_1+d^1|_2)-\beta_1(d^0|_1+d^0|_2)-\alpha_1A(d^1|_1+d^1|_2)=$$
$$=\biggl((1+\beta_2)d^1|_1-\beta_1d^0|_1-\alpha_1Ad^1|_1\biggr)+\biggl ((1+\beta_2)d^1|_2-\beta_1d^0|_2-\alpha_1Ad^1|_2\biggr)=$$ $$=d^2|_1+d^2|_2.$$

We now show that the statement of the lemma holds for arbitrary $k$. By the inductive hypothesis for iteration numbers $k\!-\!2$ and $k\!-\!1$, we have:
$$d^{k-2}=d^{k-2}|_1+d^{k-2}|_2,\ d^{k-1}=d^{k-1}|_1+d^{k-1}|_2,$$
hence
$$d^k=(1+\beta_k)d^{k-1}-\beta_{k-1}d^{k-2}-\alpha_{k-1}Ad^{k-1}=$$ $$=(1+\beta_k)(d^{k-1}|_1+d^{k-1}|_2)-\beta_{k-1}(d^{k-2}|_1+d^{k-2}|_2)-$$
$$-\alpha_{k-1}A(d^{k-1}|_1+d^{k-1}|_2)=\biggl((1+\beta_k)d^{k-1}|_1-\beta_{k-1}d^{k-2}|_1-\alpha_{k-1}Ad^{k-1}|_1\biggr)+$$
$$+\biggl ((1+\beta_k)d^{k-1}|_2-\beta_{k-1}d^{k-2}|_2-\alpha_{k-1}Ad^{k-1}|_2\biggr)=d^k|_1+d^k|_2.$$

Thus, we have shown that $d^k=d^k|_1+d^k|_2$ for $b\!=\!b|_1+b|_2$. The case of $b$ with an arbitrary number of nonzero components
$$b\!=(b_1,\dots,b_n)=\!\sum\limits_{i=1}^nb|_i,$$
where $b|_i\!=\!b_i\cdot e_i$, is treated similarly. As a result, we obtain
$$d^k=\sum\limits_{i=1}^nd^k|_i.$$

Since for $\varepsilon^k$ expression~(9) is completely analogous to~(6), it also holds that
$$\varepsilon^k=\sum\limits_{i=1}^n\varepsilon^k|_i,$$
and therefore the statement of the lemma is proved. \qed
<!-- end head-6 -->
<!-- head-7: body_md -->
{\it After the $k$-th CG iteration, we have:}
<!-- end head-7 -->
<!-- head-8: body_md -->
Since by Lemma~1, if $\ell(i,j)\!>\!k$, then for the right-hand side $b|_i\!=\!b_i\cdot e_i$ we have
$$d_j^k=d_j^k|_i=0,\quad \varepsilon_j^k=\varepsilon_j^k|_i=0.$$
Since by Lemma~2
$$d_j^k=\sum\limits_{i=1}^nd_j^k|_i,\quad \varepsilon_j^k=\sum\limits_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_j^k|_i,$$
the statement of Lemma~3 holds. \qed
<!-- end head-8 -->
<!-- head-9: body_md -->
{\it Errors arising from round-off errors in the $i$-th component of the search direction vector at the $k_1$-th CG iteration affect the error in the computation of the $j$-th component of the search direction vector, i.e., give a nonzero contribution to it, no earlier than at iteration $k_2\!=\!k_1+\ell(i,j)$.}
<!-- end head-9 -->
<!-- head-10: body_md -->
{\it For the round-off error $\varepsilon^t\!=\!\varepsilon^{t,t}$ present at the $t$-th iteration, the support of $\varepsilon^{t,k}$ is contained in the union of the $(k\!-\!1)$-neighborhoods of all vertices from $\mathrm{supp}(b)$, which means that the error propagated from iteration $t$ to iteration $k$ cannot extend beyond a distance of $k\!-\!1$ edges from the initial support.}
<!-- end head-10 -->
<!-- head-11: body_md -->
Despite the fact that for matrices with extended star graphs the condition number decreases as the diameter increases (Table 1), while for Laplacians, on the contrary, it increases (Table 3), in both cases the iteration number $N_{\mathrm{div}}$ increases with the diameter. That is, when considering these two cases together, there is no correlation between a~spectral characteristic such as the condition number and the divergence point. In contrast, there is a clear correlation between the topological characteristic --- the diameter $\mathcal{D}$ and effective diameter $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ --- and the divergence, and the dependence of the divergence iteration number $N_{\mathrm{div}}$ on $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is direct (positive).
<!-- end head-11 -->
